# Roadmap

pitfight (formerly the working name bot-arena; CLI command `pit`): a Core War-style programming game. Players write small bots for a tiny virtual machine; the bots share a circular memory arena and try to make each other crash. v1 is the ISA spec, assembler, deterministic VM and arena, tournament runner, replay format, and terminal and web viewers, in Go (standard library only) with a plain JavaScript + canvas web viewer. Source: PROJECT.md and the owner decisions of 2026-10-15 (C26-C37).

## Goals

Goal records C01-C07 come from PROJECT.md Goals. The open decisions, first filed as assumptions C20-C25, were settled by the owner on 2026-10-15 in S01 as decisions C26-C33 (name, ISA, core language, replay format, default match parameters, visualizer priority, license, CI deferred), with constraints C34-C37 (in-repo Go caches and local checks, implementer-recorded interface details, determinism rules, Go fuzzing).

### C01 Small, well-specified instruction set with a written spec

A small, well-specified instruction set with a written spec. Compatibility with the Redcode standard vs a new ISA is an open decision. (PROJECT.md Goals 1)

### C02 Assembler with labels, expressions and line-numbered errors

An assembler with labels, expressions, and clear error messages with line numbers. (PROJECT.md Goals 2)

### C03 Deterministic VM

The same bots, seed and config always give the same result, which makes replays and tests possible. (PROJECT.md Goals 3)

### C04 Arena with seeded placement, round-robin scheduling, cycle limit and tie rule

An arena with N bots, random non-overlapping start positions from a seed, round-robin process scheduling, a cycle limit and a defined tie rule. (PROJECT.md Goals 4)

### C05 Reproducible tournament runner with scoreboard

Round-robin over many seeds, a scoreboard, reproducible results. (PROJECT.md Goals 5)

### C06 Terminal and web visualizer of recorded replays

A terminal view and a web view of memory ownership and execution pointers, with step, play, pause and seek on recorded replays. (PROJECT.md Goals 6)

### C07 Compact versioned replay format

Compact, versioned, and able to drive the visualizer without re-simulating. (PROJECT.md Goals 7)

## Constraints

### C12 VM core is pure

The VM core has no I/O, no clocks, and uses seeded RNG only for placement. Everything else wraps it. (PROJECT.md Architecture sketch)

### C13 Every dependency needs owner approval

Standard library first. Every third-party Go module, toolchain (including tsc for TypeScript), wasm toolchain or JS package needs owner approval with a stated reason and a FLOSS license. The Go toolchain itself (go1.27.2) and its stock GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm target are approved by C28. (PROJECT.md Dependency / licensing notes, Risks: Toolchain; updated for C28)

### C14 Do not bundle existing warriors until licensing is checked

ICWS standards and existing warriors are public material, but their licensing has to be checked before bundling any existing warriors. Not verified yet. (PROJECT.md Dependency / licensing notes)

### C34 Go caches stay in the repo; local checks

Owner decision 2026-10-15 (carried over from the owner's sibling project). `scripts/env.sh` exports GOCACHE, GOMODCACHE, GOPATH, GOTMPDIR and TMPDIR under a gitignored `.cache/` in the repo, plus GOTOOLCHAIN=local and GOPROXY=off. Every Go command runs with it sourced (`. scripts/env.sh && go ...`). The project checks are `go test ./...`, `go vet ./...` and `gofmt -l cmd internal` (must print nothing).

### C35 Implementer decides unfixed interface details and records them

Owner decision 2026-10-15 (standing rule). Interface details not fixed by PROJECT.md or a catalog decision (for example package APIs, CLI flags and output formats, syntax details) are decided by the slice implementer and recorded in the catalog as a decision with a one-line reason. The reviewer checks each one.

### C36 Determinism: no map iteration in core; in-repo seeded PRNG

Owner decision 2026-10-15. No map iteration in the VM or arena core (Go map order is randomized). Randomness comes only from an in-repo seeded PRNG with a fixed, documented algorithm, not math/rand or math/rand/v2, so results and replays survive Go upgrades. Extends C12 and C03.

### C37 Use Go built-in fuzzing where natural

Owner decision 2026-10-15. Go's built-in fuzzing (`go test -fuzz`) needs no dependency. Use it for the assembler and VM where a slice benefits. Fuzz targets keep a seed corpus so plain `go test ./...` runs them as regular tests.

### C26 Name: pitfight, CLI command pit

Owner decision 2026-10-15. The project is named pitfight (formerly the placeholder bot-arena). The CLI command is `pit` (PROJECT.md examples that use `arena` become `pit`, e.g. `pit run imp.s dwarf.s --seed 1`). Go module path: github.com/squalor-xyz/pitfight. Replaces assumption C20.

Owner decision 2026-10-15. Accepted: an original ISA strongly inspired by Redcode semantics. Redcode compatibility may come later as a mode. Replaces assumption C21.

JS tests use node:test from the installed Node (no npm packages). Live in-browser matches, if needed, use Go's stock GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm build.

Owner decision 2026-10-15. Accepted: versioned JSON lines for v1. Replaces assumption C23.

Owner decision 2026-10-15. Accepted: start from Redcode '94 hill norms (core 8000, cycles 80000, max processes 8000). Still UNVERIFIED: the match-rules slice must verify these against a source. Replaces assumption C24.

Owner decision 2026-10-15. Accepted: terminal viewer first, web viewer second. Replaces assumption C25.

### C39 No database in v1; SQLite proposed for the hill

Owner decision 2026-10-15: v1 keeps match state in memory (pure VM, C36) and replays and tournament results as JSON-lines files (C29). No database dependency in v1. The hill slice (S19) proposes SQLite through a cgo-free driver (ncruces/go-sqlite3 or modernc.org/sqlite; confirm license) as the first non-stdlib dependency, for owner approval then. DuckDB or the sqlite3 CLI may analyse the JSONL files externally, with no code dependency.

### C40 pit usage handling: stderr+exit 2 for no args or unknown subcommand, help on stdout

Implementer decision under C35 (S02). `pit` with no arguments prints usage to stderr and exits 2; `pit help` prints usage to stdout and exits 0; an unknown subcommand prints `pit: unknown subcommand "X"`, a blank line and the usage to stderr, exit 2. The usage lists asm, run, tourney, view and help as planned, and states exit codes 0 success, 2 usage error (1 is reserved for a failed operation in later slices). Planned subcommands that are not built yet also report unknown. Reason: it matches the slice text and the shell convention that usage errors are 2 and requested help is 0; the planned-not-built case disappears as each subcommand lands.

### C41 scripts/env.sh needs bash or zsh and refuses to run outside a repo root

Implementer decision under C35 (S02), accepted by the owner 2026-10-15, overriding the slice's 'POSIX sh, no bashisms' text. A sourced POSIX script cannot learn its own path, so env.sh reads BASH_SOURCE or zsh's %x, derives the repo root from it, clears CDPATH for the cd, and exports nothing and creates nothing unless that root holds go.mod and scripts/env.sh (otherwise it prints an error and returns 1; dash fails the same way). It is sourced by absolute path from anywhere. Reason: the cache directories must follow the checkout (each worktree has its own .cache/) and a wrong or copied env.sh must never write Go caches elsewhere. env.sh does not set GOFLAGS=-modcacherw (the module has no dependencies); a slice that adds an approved dependency should revisit that.

### C42 LICENSE left absent; pending state recorded in AGENTS.md and NOTICE; SPDX header on Go and shell files

Implementer decision under C35 and C32 (S02). LICENSE is not created because the owner has not supplied the AGPL-3.0 text; AGENTS.md has a License section stating it is PENDING and that the text must not be written, fetched or edited, and NOTICE's last line points to it. Every Go file and scripts/env.sh start with SPDX-License-Identifier: AGPL-3.0-or-later. Reason: slice step 5 allows either outcome; the flag in both files keeps a missing LICENSE from reading as an oversight.

### C43 ISA opcode set: 15 opcodes, codes in table order, no MOD or CMP

Implementer decision under C35 (S03). Opcodes in code order: DAT MOV ADD SUB MUL DIV JMP JMZ JMN DJN SPL SEQ SNE SLT NOP (codes 0..14). No MOD, LDP, STP or CMP alias. All 7 modifiers and 8 modes are valid with every opcode. Reason: the smallest Redcode-like set that still expresses imp, bomber, replicator and scanner, which keeps the spec to a few pages (C27, PROJECT.md); the code order is the order of the Go constants in internal/isa. Defined in docs/spec/isa.md section 3.

### C44 ISA modifiers and addressing-mode tokens: A B AB BA F X I; # $ * @ { < } >

Implementer decision under C35 (S03). Modifier mnemonics A B AB BA F X I (codes 0..6) and mode tokens # $ * @ { < } > (codes 0..7), with Redcode field pairing and mode meanings; I acts as F except for MOV, SEQ and SNE, where it covers the whole cell. DAT, JMP, SPL and NOP ignore the modifier. Reason: the owner chose an ISA strongly inspired by Redcode semantics (C27); familiar tokens let later Redcode compatibility reuse them and need no new vocabulary. docs/spec/isa.md section 3.

### C45 ISA numbers: CORESIZE 1..2^20, stored values int32 in [0,CORESIZE), arithmetic in int64

Implementer decision under C35 (S03). 1 <= CORESIZE <= 1048576; Norm(x) = ((x mod N) + N) mod N in int64; stored operand values are int32 in [0,N); written values are any integer, stored as Norm. Reason: int64 intermediates make ADD, SUB and MUL (up to 2^40) overflow-free for every allowed size, and the range includes the sizes 1, 8 and 8000 that the S05 tests name. docs/spec/isa.md section 1.

### C46 ISA empty cell is DAT.F $0, $0 with writer 0; bot ids start at 1

Implementer decision under C35 (S03). A fresh core cell is DAT.F $0, $0, writer 0 (no bot); bot ids are 1 and up; the writer is metadata that no instruction reads and SEQ.I/SNE.I ignore. Every cell write, including pre-decrement, post-increment and DJN decrement writes, sets the writer to the executing bot. Reason: matches the Redcode empty cell and makes unwritten core visible to the visualizer as owner 0 without a special value. docs/spec/isa.md section 2 and 4.

### C47 ISA step semantics: A then B evaluation with snapshots, post-increments after execute

Implementer decision under C35 (S03). A step fetches a copy IR, evaluates A (with pre-decrement writes) then B, taking a snapshot of each target at evaluation time; an immediate operand targets the executing cell; both operands are always evaluated; the opcode writes at most one cell; post-increments of A then B apply after execution, even if the process dies; then the process effect is appended. Reason: one fixed order makes events and worked cases unambiguous for the VM, replay and visualizer. Post-increment timing may differ from Redcode and is flagged in the spec. docs/spec/isa.md section 4.

### C48 ISA faults: only DAT and division by zero kill; DIV writes nothing if any divisor is 0

Implementer decision under C35 (S03). A process dies only by executing DAT or by DIV with a zero divisor in any of its pairs; in that case DIV writes nothing for any pair. Every cell content is legal, so there is no illegal-instruction fault. Reason: a single all-or-nothing rule is simpler to specify and test than Redcode's per-pair partial write. docs/spec/isa.md section 5.

### C49 ISA SPL at the process limit acts as a continue-only NOP

Implementer decision under C35 (S03). SPL appends PC+1 then the A target; if the bot already has MAXPROCESSES live processes (the executing one counts), only PC+1 is appended and nothing is signalled. The value and range of MAXPROCESSES are left to the match spec (S04). Reason: a failed spawn must not kill or error the bot, and the executing process counts so the cap is exact. docs/spec/isa.md section 5.

### C50 ISA spec table format and worked-case format (parsed by S06)

Implementer decision under C35 (S03). Three tables, each with header first column Mnemonic, the exact assembler token in backticks, rows in code order from 0 (opcodes, modifiers, addressing modes); no other table starts with Mnemonic. Worked cases are tables headed Case | Setup | Before | After | Queue; the Case id is OPCODE.MODIFIER[/suffix] or a mode mnemonic[/suffix]; Setup is N=<core size>[, MAXPROCESSES=<n>]; Before lists address: cell separated by semicolons with unlisted cells empty; After lists each write in order; Queue lists the addresses appended, [] for a dead bot. Reason: S06 parses these tables, so a fixed machine-readable layout lets it check that every entry has a test. Cases were checked against a scratch reference stepper outside the repo. docs/spec/isa.md sections 3 and 6.

### C51 Match defaults confirmed: core 8000, cycle limit 80000, max processes 8000

Implementer decision under C35 (S04). Verifies C30 on 2026-10-15: all three values are stated as defaults in the ICWS'94 draft predefined variables (https://corewar.info/lexicon/94draft.htm: CORESIZE 8000, MAXCYCLES 80000, MAXPROCESSES 8000) and on the 94 Standard Hill page (http://www.corewar.info/hills/94.htm: core size 8000, max cycles 80000, max processes 8000); the pMARS manual (https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/noble/man6/pmars.6.html) confirms 8000 for -s and -p and gives no -c default. Ranges: CORESIZE 1..2^20, CYCLELIMIT 1..2^31-1, MAXPROCESSES 1..2^20, MINSEPARATION 0..2^20, SEED any uint64 (default 0). Reason: two independent public sources agree on each value, so C30 no longer needs its unverified flag. docs/spec/match.md sections 1 and 2.

### C52 Match PRNG: SplitMix64, seed uint64, rejection-sampled Draw(n)

Implementer decision under C35 and C36 (S04). Generator is fixed-increment SplitMix64 (state += 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15; two xor-shift-multiply rounds with 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9 and 0x94D049BB133111EB; final xor-shift 31), seed any uint64 including 0, all arithmetic modulo 2^64. Draw(n) for uint64 n>=1 rejects outputs below (2^64-n) mod n, so there is no modulo bias, and always consumes at least one output. Reason: a few lines of integer-only code with one 64-bit state and a published public-domain reference (https://prng.di.unimi.it/splitmix64.c), and rejection sampling removes modulo bias at the cost of a rule that is still easy to state exactly. Test vectors for seeds 0, 1 and 2^64-1 and rejection cases are in docs/spec/match.md section 4.

### C53 Tie rule: sole survivor wins; otherwise a tie among the last live bots

Implementer decision under C35 and C38 (S04). After the last cycle, exactly one live bot wins; two or more survivors at the cycle limit tie (tied = survivors); no survivor (all remaining bots died in the last cycle) is a tie among the bots live at the start of that cycle. No tiebreak by process count or owned cells. Reason: it keeps the pMARS manual's 'single warrior remains' win and 'both lasted until time-out' tie, and treats bots that die in the same complete cycle as equal because each took the same number of steps. docs/spec/match.md section 8.

### C54 Default min separation: 100 empty cells between neighbouring bots

Implementer decision under C35 and C38 (S04). MINSEPARATION is the minimum count of unowned cells between the end of one bot's block and the start of the next, going around the circular core; default 100, range 0..2^20. Placement is possible if and only if total bot length + bots * MINSEPARATION <= CORESIZE, else the error 'placement impossible: ...'. Reason: 100 is the default of the pMARS -d option and ICWS'94 draft MINDISTANCE (https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/noble/man6/pmars.6.html), which pMARS measures between the first instructions of two warriors; pitfight deliberately counts empty cells between blocks instead, which makes impossibility an exact sum test independent of bot length and is stricter than 100 start-to-start. docs/spec/match.md sections 2 and 6.

### C55 Placement algorithm: shuffle, rotation, sequential gap draws; no retries

Implementer decision under C35 (S04). With the seeded generator: Fisher-Yates shuffle of bot ids (draws Draw(i+1) for i=K-1..1), rotation Draw(CORESIZE), then gaps g[k]=Draw(R+1) for k=0..K-2 from remaining slack R with the last gap taking the rest, start of each bot = previous start + length + MINSEPARATION + gap; 2K-1 draws, always made. Reason: it is deterministic and bounded, never needs a retry loop, and is exact for any input that passes the feasibility sum, so two implementations agree; the gap distribution is documented as non-uniform. Worked placements and impossible cases in docs/spec/match.md section 6.

### C56 Turn order: all live bots step once per cycle in ascending id; match ends at end of cycle

Implementer decision under C35 and C38 (S04). A cycle is one step for each bot live at its start, in ascending bot id (ids = input order, not rotated); the match ends after the first cycle that leaves at most one live bot or that is cycle CYCLELIMIT; at least 2 and at most 2^20 bots; loaded cells carry the owner's bot id as writer; each bot starts with one process at its entry offset. Result fields: cycles, survivors, outcome (win or tie), winner, tied. Reason: it follows the pMARS definition of a cycle as one execution of each warrior and checking at the cycle end gives every bot the same number of steps; fixed id order is the simplest rule and fairness across orders is left to the tournament runner. docs/spec/match.md sections 5, 7 and 8.

### C57 isa package API: Opcode/Modifier/Mode uint8 types with Op*/Mod*/Mode* constants in spec order, Opcodes/Modifiers/Modes lists, String() mnemonics, Cell{Opcode,Modifier,AMode,AValue int32,BMode,BValue int32,Writer uint32}, EmptyCell

Plain typed constants and exported slices give later enumeration tests and the assembler one source for codes and mnemonics; int32 values and uint32 writer match isa.md section 1-2; no maps (C36).

### C58 vm core API: NewCore(size) (*Core, error) with ErrCoreSize, Size, Norm(int64) int32, Read(int64) Cell, Write(int64, Cell, bot uint32)

Addresses are int64 and Core.Norm is the single normalization (spec section 1), so sums cannot overflow and callers need no pre-reduction; Write sets the writer from the bot argument, Read never changes it; out-of-range size is an error rather than a panic.

### C59 vm operand API: Core.Resolve(pc, mode, value, bot) (Operand{Target, Snapshot, Post}, error) and Core.ApplyPostInc(PostInc, bot)

Splitting evaluation from post-increment lets S06 follow isa.md section 4 (evaluate A, evaluate B, execute, then post-increments on the field as it is in the core then); Resolve applies pre-decrements immediately as bot and returns ErrBadMode for a mode code above 7 instead of panicking.

### C60 VM execution and process queue API

S06 implementer decision under C35: Core.NewQueue(max, pcs...) returns (*Queue,error), normalizes initial addresses, validates MAXPROCESSES 1..2^20 and initial count, and copies input; Queue exposes Len, Dead and caller-owned Addresses. Core.Step(queue, bot, events) appends value events and executes one FIFO process, with dead queues a no-op. Queue uses a circular slice bounded by max for O(1) removal/requeue. Queues belong to their creating core and must not be copied; Step requires valid ISA codes and normalized cell fields and a nonzero bot id, matching the spec domain. Reason: arena can own one queue per bot, preserve deterministic FIFO order, and reuse its event buffer without shifting up to a million processes each turn.

### C61 VM integer event records and ordering

S06 implementer decision under C35: Event contains Kind (uint8 EventKind: CellWrite=0, ProcessSpawn=1, ProcessDeath=2), Bot uint32, PC int32, Address int32 and Cell isa.Cell. CellWrite holds the complete post-write cell including writer; process events have zero Cell. PC identifies the executed instruction, Address the written cell, child PC or dead PC. Only actual SPL child creation emits spawn; continuations and denied spawns emit nothing. All cell writes, including equal-value writes, appear in spec phase order; process events follow A/B post-increments. Reason: plain integer values retain intermediate writes for replay without I/O or clocks; caller-owned buffers avoid imposing event storage on the VM.
